pairs.rationale: The preceding account names Porcius Festus as Felix's successor; Festus now arrives in the province and travels to Jerusalem. This establishes the change of governor behind the visit without independently repeating its three-day interval.

Chief-priestly and Jewish leaders again bring Paul's case before the governor. The earlier delegation names Ananias, elders and Tertullus before Felix; the new delegation is described differently before Festus, without identifying every participant as the same person.

Both plots use a requested transfer of Paul as an opportunity to kill him en route. The earlier conspirators approach priests and elders through a proposed council examination; the later request is made to Festus. The plots and stages are not collapsed.

Festus's announced return to Caesarea is followed by his actual descent there and the tribunal hearing. The later narrative states a stay of no more than eight or ten days and a hearing the day after his descent, rather than independently measuring soon.

Festus invites influential accusers to go down with him and accuse Paul if there is wrongdoing; Jerusalem accusers subsequently appear and bring serious accusations. The narrator adds that they cannot prove them, so the invitation does not itself establish guilt.

Festus later recounts the same next-day tribunal appearance after the parties gather at Caesarea. This is his retrospective summary of the hearing, not a second hearing or an erasure of the preceding Jerusalem stay.

The narrator says the new accusations cannot be proved; at the earlier hearing Paul himself had said his accusers could not present proof. The shared lack-of-proof issue has different immediate speakers and hearings.

Paul earlier denies causing disputes or a crowd in the temple, synagogues or city and challenges the evidence; he now denies offenses against Jewish law, temple and Caesar. The earlier defense supports the related temple-and-conduct dispute without reproducing all three new categories.

Festus later repeats his question about a Jerusalem hearing. The narrator here states his wish to gain favor, whereas his own retelling presents uncertainty about investigating the matters. The different accounts of motive are preserved.

Paul's assertion that he stands before Caesar's tribunal leads into his explicit appeal and Festus's acceptance of it. This connects the stated forum with the narrated appeal, without deriving a complete Roman jurisdictional rule from the exchange.

Festus's later summary directly recalls Paul's appeal and the resulting custody pending an imperial decision. Paul's willingness to die is conditional on an actual death-worthy offense, not an admission that he committed one.

Agrippa's later statement that Paul could have been released without his appeal looks back to the accepted Caesar appeal here. It is a counterfactual comment after the hearing, not a narrated release or a decision by Caesar.

Agrippa and Bernice arrive to greet Festus and later participate in the hearing. The intervening account says they stayed several days, and the next-day hearing follows the promise in25:22, not an explicit day-after-arrival interval. Their repeated names establish the visitor-to-audience connection without adding a family or marital relationship.
Festus describes Paul as a prisoner left by Felix; the preceding narrative explicitly says Felix left Paul bound when Festus succeeded him. This is a direct custody-and-succession recap.

Festus summarizes the Jerusalem leaders' case and request for condemnation. The earlier narration gives their chief-priestly and leading-men delegation, requested Jerusalem transfer and concealed ambush plan. His retelling does not repeat every narrated purpose or use an identical group description.

Festus describes a custom of facing accusers and allowing a defense; the earlier hearing shows accusers asserting their case before the governor signals Paul to answer. This concrete procedural parallel does not independently establish the universal scope of Festus's Roman-custom statement.

Festus's first-person account of sitting on the tribunal and bringing Paul in the next day corresponds to the earlier narrated Caesarean hearing. Its no-delay wording concerns that hearing after the parties gather, not a claim that the Jerusalem visit lasted no days.

Festus says the accusers did not bring the kinds of evil charges he expected; Lysias's earlier letter likewise characterizes the case as law questions rather than a death-or-imprisonment charge. These are distinct officials' assessments, not an unqualified statement that no accusation of any kind existed.

Festus attributes to Paul the claim that the dead Jesus is alive; Paul's ensuing defense directly proclaims the Christ's suffering and resurrection. The governor is reporting Paul's position rather than himself confessing that proclamation.

The proposed Jerusalem hearing repeats Festus's earlier question. His retelling stresses investigative uncertainty; the narrator earlier specifies his wish for favor. The comparison does not replace one stated motive with the other.

The governor's report of Paul's appeal and intended transfer to Caesar recaps the appeal and accepted destination already narrated. Augustus is kept as the supplied imperial designation; no unnamed emperor is identified by adding outside chronology.

Agrippa's wish to hear Paul and Festus's promise of tomorrow are followed by the next-day assembly and Paul's being brought in. The narrative connection concerns the appointed hearing, not an assumption that Agrippa already accepted Paul's message.

Paul's being brought before the assembled hearing is followed by Agrippa granting him permission to defend himself. This connects the formal presentation with the actual speaking opportunity; the later verse does not independently repeat the pomp or all civic attendees.

Festus reports petitions and cries that Paul ought not to live; the Jerusalem crowd earlier cried to remove him from the earth because he ought not to live. The concrete death-demand wording corresponds, without proving the identities or total extent of every group Festus describes.

Festus's no-death-worthy-offense assessment is followed by the hearing party's comment that Paul deserves neither death nor imprisonment. The latter adds imprisonment and discusses the appeal; neither passage narrates the emperor's eventual judgment.

Festus needs something definite to write when sending Paul onward; the earlier transfer already included Lysias's official letter stating his assessment, law-related accusations and reasons for sending Paul to Felix. The writers, recipients and stages differ, and the letter remains its author's account.

The earlier official transfer letter actually accompanies the prisoner with an account of the case and charges; Festus now explains why sending a prisoner without indicating charges seems unreasonable. This is a concrete documentary-practice parallel, not independent proof of every Roman legal requirement.

Paul receives permission and uses a hand gesture before a defense in both scenes. Acts 21 describes motioning from the steps before a Hebrew address; Acts 26 says he stretched out his hand before Agrippa. The gestures, venues and stated language details are not made identical.

Paul positively introduces his defense before Agrippa, as he earlier cheerfully defended himself before Felix. The adjoining explanations appeal to each hearer's relevant experience; they are courteous speech openings in distinct hearings, addressing Agrippa the king and Felix the governor.

Paul bases his request for Agrippa's patient hearing on familiarity with Jewish customs and disputes; the earlier defense appeals to Felix's many years judging the nation. These are Paul's stated assessments of different officials' experience, not identical credentials.

Paul's earlier account explicitly distinguishes birth in Tarsus from upbringing in Jerusalem under Gamaliel. That clarifies his present Jerusalem-youth background without converting it into a Jerusalem birthplace or independently proving that every Jew knew his history.

Paul likewise identifies himself as a Pharisee with respect to law in the epistle and recalls persecuting the Church. The letter adds lineage and other self-descriptions; it does not independently demonstrate the present claim about all earlier witnesses or rank every Jewish party's strictness.

Paul earlier declares before the council that he is judged concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead. His present trial explanation again centers on hope in God's ancestral promise, developed into the resurrection question immediately afterward.

Before Felix Paul likewise connects worship of the fathers' God, law and prophets with hope in resurrection. This supports the shared ancestral-worship-and-hope argument, without independently establishing the exact scope of the twelve-tribes or night-and-day claim.

Both arguments challenge disbelief in resurrection in connection with the risen Christ. Corinthians explicitly reasons from denying resurrection to denying Christ's raising; Acts poses the question to this hearing's audience. The audiences and full argument forms differ.

The epistle likewise recalls Paul as formerly a persecutor and violent abuser acting in ignorance and unbelief. This corresponds to his former belief that he should oppose Jesus's name, not a declaration that such opposition was right because he once thought it necessary.

The earlier narrative records Saul approving Stephen's killing and imprisoning men and women. Paul now recalls imprisonments and his vote against those being killed. The comparison does not turn approval into proof of a formal council seat or identify every unnamed victim.

Paul earlier tells the Lord of imprisoning and beating believers in synagogues and approving Stephen's killing. These fit his present persecution recollection; tried to compel blasphemy and pursuit of foreign cities are additional details, not reported successful apostasy in every victim.

The earlier narrative describes Saul requesting the high priest's letters for Damascus in order to bind followers of the Way. Paul now recounts the same journey under chief-priestly authority, with the authorization phrased differently.

The other defense likewise places the heavenly light on the Damascus journey about noon. Acts 26 additionally says brighter than the sun and surrounding companions; Acts 22's selected wording says around me. The descriptions are not silently expanded into identical accounts.

The repeated Saul, Saul, why persecute Me voice identifies the same encounter. Acts 9 describes Saul falling and his companions standing speechless; Acts 26 says all fell and specifies Hebrew and the goads saying. No unreported falling-and-rising sequence or missing goads clause is supplied to harmonize them.

Both accounts give Saul's Who art Thou, Lord question and Jesus's identification as the One he persecutes. This is a direct retelling of the encounter, not a separate naming ceremony or a change from Saul to Paul at that moment.

Both accounts describe appointment to witness what Paul has seen and heard. Acts 22 places that explanation in Ananias's speech in Damascus; Acts 26 presents the Lord's direct commission with future appearances. The speaker arrangement and additional clauses are retained rather than equated word for word.

Paul's other defense also quotes the Lord sending him to the Gentiles. Acts 22 locates that saying in the Jerusalem-temple trance after his return, whereas this commission is presented in the Damascus-road account. The shared sending does not force both sayings into one unreported chronology.

The commission to open eyes and turn people from darkness closely recalls the divinely called servant's light-for-nations task of opening blind eyes and releasing those in darkness. Isaiah's physical captivity imagery and Acts's forgiveness-and-faith explanation remain distinct, and Isaiah does not name Paul.

Both passages join light, deliverance from hostile authority, forgiveness and a share among holy people. Acts names Satan's authority and sanctification by faith in Jesus; Colossians thanks the Father for rescue from darkness and transfer into His Son's kingdom. The specific agents and formulations are preserved.

The earlier narrative shows Saul immediately proclaiming Jesus and demonstrating Him to be the Christ after the encounter. This supplies a concrete initial missionary response corresponding to Paul's claim of obedience, without purporting to list every subsequent action.

Barnabas's report mentions Paul's bold Damascus proclamation, and the following narrative places his bold witness in Jerusalem. These match the first named centers here; the selected earlier passage does not cover the entire Judean and Gentile itinerary.

Paul's call to repent, turn to God and do works worthy of repentance parallels John's instruction to produce fruits worthy of repentance. The concrete repentance-and-fitting-conduct connection does not make works and fruits identical English wording or turn this into the same sermon.

The temple seizure and attempted killing are directly narrated earlier. That account reports accusations about people, law and temple and explicitly calls Trophimus's temple entry a supposition; Paul's present summary relates the attack to his ministry. No alleged Gentile entry is promoted to fact.

Jesus's teaching likewise places His suffering, resurrection and proclamation to the nations within the fulfillment of Moses and the prophets. Paul appeals to that scriptural framework for his testimony; the passages do not independently identify every prophetic text or repeat an identical message.

Christ's priority in resurrection corresponds to the epistle's raised-Christ firstfruits language and its ordered resurrection argument. Acts also speaks of proclaiming light; Corinthians develops Adam, Christ and those belonging to Him rather than narrating the present hearing.

The proclamation of light to the people and Gentiles corresponds to the servant's task concerning Jacob's tribes, Israel's dispersion and light for nations. Acts identifies the Christ's mission; Isaiah's fuller promise does not name Paul or provide this hearing's resurrection wording.
Festus's accusation of madness is directly answered by Paul's denial and claim to truth and sound judgment. This is an explicit report-and-rebuttal pair, not the narrator's medical diagnosis of Paul.

Paul's not-mad response specifically negates Festus's preceding characterization. The contrast records the two speakers' claims about his defense and does not independently settle a clinical question.

Cleopas likewise treats recent events concerning Jesus as widely knowable when questioning the unrecognized visitor. Paul appeals to Agrippa's knowledge and the events' public character. The different encounters do not prove that every individual knew them or identify Cleopas with another similarly named person.

The question about Agrippa believing the prophets follows Paul's explicit claim that Moses and the prophets foretold the Christ's suffering and resurrection message. This connects the appeal to its stated scriptural premise; Paul's I know claim is not a recorded Christian profession by the king.

The Christian designation in Agrippa's response corresponds to the narrative's earlier account of disciples first being called Christians at Antioch. His supplied with-so-little wording is not rewritten as a statement that he almost converted or actually became Christian.

Paul's whether with little or much directly takes up Agrippa's with so little response, then extends the Christian wish from the king to all hearers while excepting his bonds. This is a specific rhetorical reply and prayer, not a report that the hearers converted.

The king, governor, Bernice and fellow hearers rise at the close of the hearing whose assembled scene earlier names Agrippa, Bernice and the civic audience. The repeated party frames this same event without independently repeating every attendee's rank or implying an acquittal at their rising.

After withdrawing, the hearers find nothing deserving death or imprisonment; Festus had earlier found nothing deserving death. The later private conversation adds imprisonment to the assessment and is not itself a narrated release order.

Agrippa's conditional statement refers directly to Paul's accepted Caesar appeal. The earlier exchange explains that reference, but neither text records withdrawal of the appeal, actual release or the emperor's final decision.
